rv.q: Ms. McDormand gives a performance of such fierce, clear-eyed intelligence that she makes you feel you're witnessing the birth of a legend.
By the time Harris delivers Miss Helen's final speech about her quixotic artistic quest, you may find yourself reaching for a tissue rather than your cellphone.
Theatre Company's somewhat sleepy but still satisfying production of "The Road to Mecca" opened Tuesday at the Theater featuring Carla Gugino, Jim Dale and the luminous Rosemary Harris.
Alas, in Gordon Edelstein's cautious, small-scaled staging in the large Theatre, such complex intimacies strain to be heard, much less understood.
But a compelling case is made for this wordy 1984 drama about individual and artistic freedom only deep into its second act.
Everyone and everything feels too far apart in this Mecca; actors can’t seem to get a firm grip on one another and nothing ever feels the least bit urgent.
You may be inclined to forgive the play’s longueurs in exchange for this eloquent reminder that all art, to some extent, is outsider art.
Harris is riveting, even when sitting still and absorbing the other two characters' thoughts.
Harris, still luminous at 84 years old, caps a brilliant career with a deeply felt performance.
Her delicate and detailed performance of a woman battling the darkness that can seep into one's soul shimmers with its own bright light.
It works sometimes, yet there is a sense that the play traverses the same ground over and over again.
Despite sterling performances from Carla Gugino, Jim Dale, and the luminous Rosemary Harris, it's a bit of a slog to 'Mecca'

Harris is a luminous and appealing Helen, and Dale gives a wisely subdued, nuanced portrayal of Marius. Gugino is a bit overstated at times as Elsa, but she also gives the play a welcome jolt of energy.
Yet this Road to Mecca, at the Theatre through March 4, is long, winding, and, in the end, more than a little unsatisfying.
Although the production features a fine cast including Rosemary Harris, Jim Dale and Carla Gugino, it's about as exciting overall as watching paint dry.
Harris is a transcendent, complex Helen, subtly displaying her strengths, weaknesses and insecurities.

This year is playwright Athol Fugard’s 80th birthday and the first production in New York to be mounted in the honor of this South African trailblazer is, appropriately enough, about the bravery of artists.

cn.t: Harris shines in this wordy Fugard drama, but critics find the production a slow, talky slog that struggles to build theatrical urgency in the oversized venue, with only patient viewers rewarded by its eventual humanity.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
